now.open_questions: Can helium and neon ever form stable compounds in normal conditions? Recent calculations suggest Na2He may be stable at very high pressures (predicted 2014, possibly observed 2017). Can predictive computational chemistry guide synthesis of new noble gas compounds?

items.reflection: From 1933 to 1962, the prediction that xenon should form compounds was on the books. No one tried seriously for nearly 30 years because everyone knew noble gases were inert. How often does scientific orthodoxy keep researchers from attempting experiments that turn out to be both feasible and revolutionary?

moments.title: Natural isotopes and transmutation
moments.body:
Rutherford in 1919 demonstrates the first artificial transmutation: alpha + nitrogen → oxygen-17 + proton. Aston perfects the mass spectrograph (1919) and shows elements are mixtures of isotopes. Chadwick discovers the neutron (1932).

By 1933 the elementary nuclear physics is in place, but all known radioactive elements are still naturally occurring. The Joliot-Curies will change that.
moments.takeaway: Nuclear bombardment can change elements. But all known radioactive isotopes remain natural.

moments.title: Joliot-Curies miss the neutron and the positron
moments.body:
Working at the Radium Institute, the Joliot-Curies observe a 'mysterious radiation' from beryllium when bombarded with alpha particles. They publish — but interpret it as gamma rays. Chadwick reads their paper, immediately realises it's a neutral particle of nucleon mass, and discovers the neutron.

They also observe positrons emitted from beryllium and aluminium under alpha bombardment — but again interpret them as protons. Anderson (Caltech, 1932) wins the credit for the positron.

Twice missed in 18 months.
moments.takeaway: Even great experimentalists can misinterpret their own data. The Joliot-Curies are determined not to miss the next one.

moments.title: Artificial radioactivity discovered
moments.body:
On 11 January 1934, the Joliot-Curies bombard aluminium foil with alpha particles from a polonium source. They notice that after removing the polonium source, the aluminium continues to emit radiation — for several minutes — before going quiet.

They have created phosphorus-30, a radioactive isotope that does not occur in nature. Its half-life is 2.5 minutes; it decays by positron emission to silicon-30.

Alpha + aluminium-27 → phosphorus-30 + neutron.
moments.takeaway: Radioactivity can be made on demand. Any element could potentially be made radioactive by nuclear bombardment.

moments.title: Nobel Prize in Chemistry
moments.body:
The Joliot-Curies share the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. They are the second married couple to share a Nobel — the first being Marie and Pierre Curie in 1903. Irène is the daughter of those laureates.

Marie Curie had died of aplastic anaemia in July 1934, six months after her daughter's discovery and one year before the Nobel announcement.
moments.takeaway: A second-generation Nobel. The Curie/Joliot-Curie family becomes the most-laureated in scientific history.

now.title: Artificial isotopes today
now.body:
About 3000 isotopes are known across 118 elements; most are made artificially. Medical isotopes (Tc-99m for SPECT imaging, F-18 for PET, I-131 for thyroid therapy) are routinely made in reactors and cyclotrons.

Fermi extended the Joliot-Curies' work using neutrons instead of alphas (Rome, 1934 onwards) and produced many new isotopes — and (unknowingly) the first products of uranium fission, recognised as such by Hahn, Strassmann and Meitner in 1938.
now.open_questions: How far can the chart of nuclides extend? Where are the limits of nuclear stability (the 'drip lines')? Can we synthesise long-lived superheavy elements at the predicted 'island of stability'?

items.reflection: Both Joliot-Curies died of radiation-related illness — Irène of leukaemia in 1956, Frédéric of liver disease in 1958. Two generations of Curie women died of their work. How do we evaluate the moral economy of scientific discovery when the discoverers themselves are killed by what they uncover?

moments.title: Crookes predicts a nitrogen crisis
moments.who: William Crookes, presidential address to the British Association
moments.body:
Sir William Crookes gives a famous address: 'The Wheat Problem'. He argues that the world's reliance on natural nitrogen fertilisers (Chilean nitrate, guano) cannot keep up with population growth. By the 1930s, he predicts, the world will face widespread famine unless chemists can fix atmospheric nitrogen.

The challenge is taken up across Europe. Several routes are tried: electric arc fixing (Birkeland-Eyde, Norway), calcium cyanamide (Frank-Caro, Germany), but all are too energy-intensive.
moments.takeaway: Civilisation's food supply is identified as a chemistry problem. The race is on.

moments.title: Haber demonstrates lab-scale ammonia synthesis
moments.body:
Haber demonstrates a tabletop apparatus that combines N2 and H2 over an osmium catalyst at high pressure (175 atm) and 550°C, producing droplets of liquid ammonia. The reaction is exothermic and gas-mole-reducing — Le Chatelier favours high pressure and low temperature, but only high temperature gives practical rates.

BASF buys the patent. Carl Bosch is assigned to scale it up.
moments.takeaway: A tabletop demonstration of the reaction every chemist had been chasing for two decades.

moments.title: Bosch builds the Oppau plant
moments.body:
Bosch and Alwin Mittasch screen thousands of catalyst formulations and settle on a promoted iron catalyst (with potassium and aluminium oxide promoters) — vastly cheaper than osmium. They engineer the high-pressure reactors, the gas-recirculation loops and the safety systems.

The Oppau plant begins producing ammonia at industrial scale in September 1913. By 1914 it produces 30 tonnes a day.
moments.takeaway: The largest chemical engineering project of its day — and a template for high-pressure synthesis ever since.

moments.title: Ammonia feeds the German war effort
moments.body:
When WWI begins, Britain's blockade cuts off German imports of Chilean nitrate. Ammonia from Haber-Bosch becomes the basis of explosives manufacture (via nitric acid and ammonium nitrate). Germany can fight on for four years rather than collapsing in months.

Haber also personally leads Germany's chemical weapons programme — chlorine gas at Ypres in April 1915, then mustard gas. His first wife Clara Immerwahr (also a chemist) shoots herself in May 1915 in apparent protest.
moments.takeaway: Industrial chemistry sustains an industrial war. The same plant that makes fertiliser makes explosives.

moments.title: Two Nobel Prizes — Haber and Bosch
moments.body:
Haber wins the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The award is intensely controversial given his role in chemical warfare. Several past laureates boycott the ceremony.

Bosch wins the 1931 Nobel Prize in Chemistry (with Friedrich Bergius) for the engineering of high-pressure chemistry. Haber, of Jewish descent, is forced out of his Berlin institute by the Nazis in 1933 and dies in 1934 en route to Cambridge.
moments.takeaway: Recognition without resolution. The science and the moral weight remain entangled.

now.title: Ammonia today
now.body:
About 180 million tonnes of ammonia are made annually worldwide. About 80 percent goes to fertilisers — feeding an estimated 3.5 to 4 billion people. The process consumes about 1-2 percent of the world's total energy and emits roughly 1.4 percent of global CO2.

Hydrogen for the process comes overwhelmingly from steam reforming of natural gas (releasing CO2). 'Green ammonia' — using hydrogen made by electrolysis with renewable electricity — is a major research and engineering target. ITER-scale ammonia plants are being planned in Australia, Saudi Arabia and Chile.
now.open_questions: Can green ammonia scale and compete with fossil-fuel ammonia on cost? Can low-temperature catalysts replace the energy-hungry Haber-Bosch conditions? Can biological nitrogen fixation (the way legumes do it via nitrogenase) be engineered into cereal crops?

items.reflection: The Haber-Bosch process feeds half the world and was central to a war that killed 17 million people. Haber's first wife killed herself in apparent protest at his role in chemical weapons. How do we hold the simultaneous truth that a single scientist enabled both humanitarian benefit on a vast scale and unprecedented military destruction?

moments.title: Avogadro's hypothesis
moments.body:
Avogadro proposes that equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain the same number of particles — and that elemental gases such as O2 are diatomic, not monatomic. The idea resolves Dalton's contradictions about water (HO vs H2O).

The paper is ignored for 50 years.
moments.takeaway: The right answer about molecules and atoms, ignored for half a century.

moments.title: Karlsruhe Congress
moments.body: At the first international chemistry conference, Cannizzaro circulates a pamphlet defending Avogadro's hypothesis. The argument persuades Mendeleev and Meyer; the periodic table follows within a decade.
moments.takeaway: The first international scientific congress saves a 49-year-old neglected idea.

moments.title: Perrin measures Avogadro's number
moments.body: Using Brownian motion, Perrin measures Avogadro's number to within 10% of the modern value. The energeticist resistance collapses; atoms are now experimental fact.
moments.takeaway: Avogadro's number measured directly — and the atomic theory is settled.

moments.title: Mole redefined
moments.body: The mole is redefined as exactly 6.02214076 × 10^23 entities — Avogadro's number is now an exact constant by definition, not measurement.
moments.takeaway: Avogadro's number becomes an exact mathematical constant of the SI.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The mole is one of seven SI base units. Modern stoichiometry, gas laws and titration calculations all rest on Avogadro's hypothesis.
now.open_questions: What are the smallest physical samples we can synthesise — single-molecule chemistry?

items.reflection: Avogadro got the right answer in 1811 and was ignored. The Karlsruhe Congress finally heard him. What does it take to overcome 50 years of neglect?

moments.title: Lewis's cubical atom
moments.body: Lewis proposes the shared-electron pair as the basic chemical bond. In a paper drafted partly on the back of an envelope, he sketches atoms as cubes with electrons at the corners and bonds as shared edges. The octet rule emerges.
moments.takeaway: The shared electron pair, drawn on an envelope, becomes the central concept in chemistry.

moments.title: Lewis's textbook
moments.body: Lewis publishes 'Valence and the Structure of Atoms and Molecules', founding modern chemical bonding theory. He also formulates the broader Lewis acid-base concept the same year.
moments.takeaway: Lewis dot structures become the universal language of bonding.

moments.title: Pauling's resonance
moments.body: Pauling's 'The Nature of the Chemical Bond' uses quantum mechanics to ground Lewis's ideas. Hybridisation, resonance and electronegativity formalise organic and inorganic structure. Pauling wins the 1954 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Quantum mechanics meets the curly arrow.

moments.title: VSEPR
moments.body: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) lets schoolchildren predict molecular geometry from Lewis structures: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, etc. Simple, predictive, brilliant.
moments.takeaway: Molecular shape becomes a back-of-envelope calculation.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Lewis structures, VSEPR and electronegativity are universal teaching tools. Quantum chemistry calculations (DFT) now compute structures of millions of molecules. Both work.
now.open_questions: How accurate can semi-empirical bonding models be made? Can ML replace DFT?

items.reflection: Lewis was nominated for 35 Nobel Prizes and never won. He died (possibly by suicide) in his lab in 1946. Why does Nobel recognition sometimes elude the obvious?

moments.title: Guldberg and Waage formalise
moments.body: Two Norwegian brothers-in-law publish the law of mass action: the rate of a reaction is proportional to the concentrations of reactants. The paper is in Norwegian; it is ignored for 13 years.
moments.takeaway: The first quantitative law of chemical equilibrium, in an obscure Norwegian journal.

moments.title: Le Chatelier's principle
moments.body: A mining engineer formulates a qualitative principle: 'If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to oppose the disturbance.' The principle is widely used in chemistry teaching ever since.
moments.takeaway: A simple qualitative principle to predict reaction shifts.

moments.title: Haber-Bosch ammonia
moments.body: Haber demonstrates ammonia synthesis from N2 and H2 at high pressure and temperature, using an osmium catalyst. Bosch scales it for industry at BASF. Le Chatelier's principle is applied at industrial scale — Haber wins the 1918 Nobel, Bosch in 1931.
moments.takeaway: Le Chatelier's principle feeds half the world.

moments.title: Nitrogen for the planet
moments.body: The Haber-Bosch process now fixes ~200 million tonnes of N per year — about half of the nitrogen in human bodies came from a Haber-Bosch reactor. It uses 1-2% of all global energy.
moments.takeaway: Le Chatelier's principle keeps the world fed.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Equilibrium calculations are central to industrial chemistry, biochemistry and climate science. Catalysis aims for green Haber-Bosch with renewable hydrogen.
now.open_questions: Can low-pressure, low-energy ammonia synthesis be commercialised?

items.reflection: Haber, the savior of agriculture, also developed chlorine gas for WWI; his wife killed herself in despair. How should we judge the morality of dual-use chemistry?

moments.title: Arrhenius's dissertation
moments.body:
Arrhenius's PhD thesis proposes that salts dissociate into ions in water. The examiners are bewildered and award the lowest passing grade. He nearly fails.

Within 20 years the theory wins the 1903 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A PhD thesis that nearly fails wins a Nobel Prize 19 years later.

moments.title: Arrhenius equation
moments.body: Arrhenius derives k = A exp(-Ea/RT). The exponential dependence of rate on temperature explains why 'a 10°C rise roughly doubles reaction rate'.
moments.takeaway: An exponential law links temperature to chemical rate.

moments.title: Transition state theory
moments.body: Eyring's transition state theory derives the Arrhenius pre-factor from statistical mechanics. Rate = (kT/h) exp(-Delta G‡/RT). The activation energy gets a structural interpretation.
moments.takeaway: Reaction rates become a problem in molecular geometry.

moments.title: Arrhenius and climate
moments.body: Arrhenius is also the first to calculate that doubling atmospheric CO2 would warm Earth by 5-6 °C (his estimate). He sees it as beneficial for Scandinavian agriculture.
moments.takeaway: The same chemist who explains kinetics also founds climate science.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Arrhenius plots (ln k vs 1/T) are standard for measuring activation energies. They underpin food preservation, drug stability, and modelling enzyme kinetics.
now.open_questions: Can computational chemistry predict activation energies to chemical accuracy (1 kcal/mol)?

items.reflection: Arrhenius's PhD examiners gave him a near-failing grade. The work won a Nobel Prize. How do you tell brilliance from nonsense when an idea is brand new?

moments.title: Fischer's lock and key
moments.body: Fischer proposes that enzymes act like locks accepting only specific substrate keys. He wins the 1902 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Enzyme specificity is geometric.

moments.title: Michaelis-Menten equation
moments.body: Michaelis (Berlin) and Menten (a Canadian doctor who traveled to Berlin to work with him) derive v = V_max[S]/(K_m + [S]) for enzyme kinetics. The equation is one of the most-used in biochemistry.
moments.takeaway: The foundational equation of enzyme kinetics — derived by a woman barred from research positions in Canada.

moments.title: Induced fit
moments.body: Koshland refines lock-and-key: enzymes change shape on binding substrate. The induced-fit model explains regulation and allostery.
moments.takeaway: Enzymes are flexible. Catalysis is dynamic.

moments.title: Catalysis at industrial scale
moments.body: Enzymes catalyse industrial processes from detergent manufacture to insulin production. Directed evolution (Arnold, 2018 Nobel) tailors enzymes to non-natural substrates.
moments.takeaway: Enzymes industrial-scale catalysis enables green chemistry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Enzyme engineering is a major field. CRISPR-Cas9 enzymes edit genomes. AlphaFold predicts enzyme structures from sequence. Directed evolution wins Nobels.
now.open_questions: Can we design enzymes for arbitrary reactions de novo?

items.reflection: Maud Menten could not get a research post in Canada because she was a woman. Why does science still credit individuals over the structures that exclude others?

moments.title: Arrhenius acids
moments.body: Arrhenius defines acids as substances that produce H+ in water; bases as substances that produce OH-. The definition works for aqueous solutions.
moments.takeaway: The first general theory of acidity.

moments.title: pH scale
moments.body: Brewing chemist Sørensen at the Carlsberg Lab defines pH = -log[H+] to quantify acidity in beer brewing. The scale becomes universal.
moments.takeaway: Beer chemistry gives us the pH scale.

moments.title: Brønsted-Lowry
moments.body: Independently, Brønsted and Lowry redefine acids as proton donors, bases as proton acceptors. The definition handles non-aqueous and gas-phase reactions.
moments.takeaway: Acid-base becomes proton transfer.

moments.title: Lewis acids
moments.body: The same year, Lewis defines acids as electron-pair acceptors. This includes proton-free Lewis acids such as BF3 and AlCl3 — the workhorses of organic synthesis.
moments.takeaway: Acid-base becomes electron-pair transfer.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: All three definitions are still used. Brønsted-Lowry dominates in aqueous chemistry; Lewis dominates in synthesis and catalysis. pH is measured in soils, blood, oceans worldwide.
now.open_questions: How will ocean acidification (current pH drop of 0.1 units) reshape marine ecosystems?

items.reflection: Three useful definitions of 'acid' coexist. Is a single 'true' definition possible — or always context-dependent?

moments.title: Rabi's molecular beam
moments.body: Rabi detects nuclear magnetic resonance in molecular beams. He wins the 1944 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: NMR is born as a precision atomic-physics technique.

moments.title: NMR in liquids and solids
moments.body: Bloch and Purcell independently detect NMR in liquids (water) and solids (paraffin). They share the 1952 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: NMR becomes useful for chemistry.

moments.title: Chemical shift discovered
moments.body: Different nuclei in different chemical environments resonate at slightly different frequencies. NMR becomes a fingerprint for organic chemistry. Spin-spin coupling reveals connectivity.
moments.takeaway: NMR is the structural workhorse of organic chemistry.

moments.title: FT-NMR and MRI
moments.who: Richard Ernst, Kurt Wüthrich, Paul Lauterbur, Peter Mansfield
moments.body: Ernst introduces Fourier-transform NMR (1991 Nobel). Wüthrich uses NMR to solve protein structures (2002 Nobel). Lauterbur and Mansfield invent MRI (2003 Nobel).
moments.takeaway: NMR earns at least four Nobel Prizes across physics, chemistry and medicine.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: NMR is ubiquitous in chemistry, biochemistry and medicine. MRI scanners use it for non-invasive imaging. Modern NMR magnets reach 28 tesla; cryogen-free NMR is emerging.
now.open_questions: Can in-cell NMR resolve native protein dynamics? Can hyperpolarised MRI image metabolism in real time?

items.reflection: NMR began as obscure atomic physics and became a hospital scanner. How often does pure physics become medicine within a generation?

moments.title: Goodyear's vulcanisation
moments.body: Goodyear accidentally drops rubber mixed with sulphur onto a hot stove. The product is stable — vulcanised rubber. He dies in debt; the company that bears his name comes later.
moments.takeaway: The first synthetic modification of a natural polymer — by accident.

moments.title: Bakelite
moments.body: Baekeland synthesises a phenol-formaldehyde resin that can be moulded. Bakelite — the first fully synthetic plastic — launches the plastics age.
moments.takeaway: The first fully synthetic plastic. The plastic age begins.

moments.title: Staudinger and macromolecules
moments.body: Staudinger proposes that polymers are giant covalent molecules. Chemists ridicule the idea: 'Dear colleague, leave the concept of large molecules well alone... no such things as macromolecules exist.' He wins the 1953 Nobel anyway.
moments.takeaway: Staudinger fights for the idea that polymers are real molecules — for 30 years.

moments.title: Nylon
moments.body: Carothers, leading DuPont's industrial research, develops nylon, neoprene and other synthetic polymers. He suffers depression and dies by suicide in 1937, before nylon is launched (1939).
moments.takeaway: Modern synthetic polymers are born in industrial labs.

moments.title: Ziegler-Natta catalysis
moments.body: Ziegler and Natta develop catalysts (now called Ziegler-Natta) for controlled polymerisation of olefins. They enable polyethylene, polypropylene and isotactic polymers. 1963 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Polymer chemistry becomes a multi-trillion-dollar industry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Plastics production is ~400 million tonnes per year. Microplastics are found in every ocean, every continent, in human blood. Biodegradable plastics are a major research field.
now.open_questions: Can biodegradable polymers replace conventional plastics at scale? How do microplastics affect health?

items.reflection: Staudinger was mocked for the idea of macromolecules; Carothers, who built modern polymer chemistry, killed himself. Why has plastic's success come at such cost?

moments.title: Rutherford transmutes nitrogen
moments.body: Rutherford fires alpha particles at nitrogen and produces oxygen and a proton. The first artificial nuclear reaction. He has accomplished alchemy.
moments.takeaway: Nuclear transmutation: an element is changed by human hand.

moments.title: Artificial radioactivity
moments.body: Marie's daughter and son-in-law produce phosphorus-30 by bombarding aluminium with alpha particles. They create the first radioactive isotope that does not occur naturally. 1935 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Radioactive isotopes can be made to order.

moments.title: Technetium synthesised
moments.body: Technetium (element 43), missing from the periodic table, is synthesised by bombarding molybdenum with deuterons. It is the first synthetic element. Today Tc-99m is the most-used isotope in nuclear medicine.
moments.takeaway: Element 43, missing from Mendeleev's table, is synthesised at last.

moments.title: Transuranic synthesis
moments.body: Neptunium (1940), plutonium (1941), and so on up to oganesson (2002) are synthesised. The periodic table grows to 118 elements — none of the heavier ones occur naturally. Element 117, tennessine, was made in just six atoms.
moments.takeaway: The periodic table is now extended atom by atom in particle accelerators.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: All transuranic elements are radioactive. Nuclear medicine uses Tc-99m, I-131, F-18 in millions of procedures annually. PET imaging requires cyclotron-produced isotopes.
now.open_questions: Is there an 'island of stability' for superheavy elements? Where does the periodic table end?

items.reflection: The Joliot-Curies died of radiation-related illness (Irène of leukaemia, Frédéric of liver disease). The price of nuclear chemistry was paid in lives.

moments.title: Sanger sequences insulin
moments.body: Sanger spends 10 years determining the amino-acid sequence of insulin — 51 residues. He shows proteins have defined sequences, not random arrangements. 1958 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Proteins have a code. The sequence determines the function.

moments.title: DNA sequencing
moments.body: Sanger develops the chain-termination ('dideoxy') method for DNA sequencing. He wins his second Nobel in 1980. The Sanger Institute is named for him.
moments.takeaway: A method for reading the genome — invented by the same man who first sequenced a protein.

moments.title: First whole genome
moments.who: Haemophilus influenzae, J. Craig Venter et al.
moments.body: The 1.8-Mb genome of a bacterium is sequenced by shotgun-sequencing. The Human Genome Project (2003) and Venter's parallel race follow.
moments.takeaway: From insulin sequence to whole genomes in 42 years.

moments.title: Next-generation sequencing
moments.body: Massively parallel sequencing brings cost from $3 billion (HGP) to under $200 per human genome (2024). Nanopore sequencing can be done on a USB stick.
moments.takeaway: Sequencing is now millions of times cheaper than 20 years ago.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Sequencing underlies modern biology, medicine, agriculture and forensics. Personal genomics is a consumer product. Liquid-biopsy cancer detection relies on sequencing.
now.open_questions: Can we sequence every species on Earth (Earth BioGenome)? Can we sequence within cells in real time?

items.reflection: Sanger won two Nobels in chemistry — alone among scientists in that respect. What enables decades-long productivity?

moments.title: Fraunhofer lines
moments.body: A self-taught optician finds hundreds of dark lines in the solar spectrum and catalogues them. The lines remain mysterious for 45 years.
moments.takeaway: The Sun's spectrum has hundreds of unexplained dark lines.

moments.title: Bunsen and Kirchhoff
moments.body: Using Bunsen's clean burner and a prism, they show each element has a fingerprint spectrum. They explain Fraunhofer lines as solar atmospheric absorption. Within months they discover caesium and rubidium.
moments.takeaway: Chemistry can now identify elements from their light.

moments.title: Helium in the Sun
moments.body: A yellow line in the solar spectrum, attributed to a new element — helium. It is not found on Earth until 1895 (Ramsay).
moments.takeaway: An element is discovered on the Sun before being found on Earth.

moments.title: Raman spectroscopy
moments.body: Raman discovers that scattered light has shifted frequencies revealing vibrational modes. He wins the 1930 Nobel — the first Asian to win a science Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Inelastic light scattering becomes a workhorse of molecular spectroscopy.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Spectroscopy (UV-Vis, IR, Raman, NMR, MS) is the chemist's primary characterisation toolkit. Modern instruments are 1000x more sensitive than 1960s versions.
now.open_questions: Can single-molecule spectroscopy become routine? Can we identify protein states in vivo?

items.reflection: Bunsen's burner, invented for clean spectroscopy, became the most iconic apparatus in school chemistry. How does pure research equipment become pedagogy?

moments.title: Freon invented
moments.body:
Midgley develops CFCs as 'safe' refrigerants. He demonstrates safety by inhaling a lungful and exhaling onto a candle to extinguish it. CFCs replace toxic ammonia and SO2 in refrigerators.

Midgley also invented leaded petrol. He has been called the single organism with the most negative impact on Earth's atmosphere.
moments.takeaway: A 'safe' invention that turns out to be catastrophic at planetary scale.

moments.title: Molina and Rowland's warning
moments.who: Mario Molina, F. Sherwood Rowland, UC Irvine
moments.body: Molina and Rowland predict that CFCs will rise to the stratosphere, be broken by UV, and release chlorine radicals that catalytically destroy ozone. The chemical industry resists. They share the 1995 Nobel with Crutzen.
moments.takeaway: Chemistry predicts a planetary disaster — and is initially dismissed by industry.

moments.title: Ozone hole discovered
moments.who: Joe Farman et al., British Antarctic Survey
moments.body: Farman's team finds Antarctic stratospheric ozone has dropped by 40%. The 'ozone hole' confirms Molina and Rowland's prediction. Satellite data, initially flagged as instrument error, had been showing the same thing.
moments.takeaway: The ozone hole is real. Even satellites had missed it because the readings looked impossible.

moments.title: Montreal Protocol
moments.body: The Montreal Protocol phases out CFCs internationally. It is signed by every UN member — the only such treaty. Ozone is now slowly recovering; full recovery is expected by ~2070.
moments.takeaway: International chemistry-led action averts a planetary disaster.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The ozone layer is recovering at ~1-3% per decade. HFCs replaced CFCs but are potent greenhouse gases; the Kigali Amendment (2016) phases them out too. Climate change still poses similar coordination problems.
now.open_questions: Can climate diplomacy match the success of the Montreal Protocol?

items.reflection: Midgley invented both leaded petrol and CFCs — both initially praised, both planetary disasters. How should we evaluate inventions whose harm is delayed by decades?

moments.title: Diels and Alder
moments.body: Diels and his student Alder discover that dienes and dienophiles react cleanly to form six-membered rings — a [4+2] cycloaddition. They win the 1950 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: One reaction builds half of the rings in synthetic organic chemistry.

moments.title: Woodward's quinine synthesis
moments.body: Robert Burns Woodward uses Diels-Alder strategically in his total synthesis of quinine, then cholesterol, then chlorophyll, then vitamin B12 (with Eschenmoser). Total synthesis becomes the ultimate art form in chemistry.
moments.takeaway: Diels-Alder enables the most spectacular total syntheses ever.

moments.title: Woodward-Hoffmann rules
moments.body: Woodward and Hoffmann derive the rules of orbital symmetry governing pericyclic reactions. Hoffmann wins the 1981 Nobel (with Fukui); Woodward had died in 1979.
moments.takeaway: Symmetry governs which cycloadditions are allowed and forbidden.

moments.title: Catalytic enantioselective Diels-Alder
moments.who: E. J. Corey, David Evans, others
moments.body: Chiral Lewis-acid catalysts produce single enantiomers from Diels-Alder reactions. Synthetic chemistry meets asymmetric synthesis.
moments.takeaway: Diels-Alder becomes stereoselective at industrial scale.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Diels-Alder is used to build natural products, pharmaceuticals (e.g. steroids), and polymers. Bioorthogonal chemistry (Bertozzi, 2022 Nobel) uses inverse-electron-demand variants to label live cells.
now.open_questions: Can the Diels-Alder be made photocatalytic and earth-abundant-metal catalysed at industrial scale?

items.reflection: One reaction — the Diels-Alder — appears in countless natural-product syntheses. Why are some reactions so disproportionately useful?

moments.title: Thomson's parabolas
moments.body: Thomson, examining canal rays, finds neon gives two parabolas — masses 20 and 22. The first evidence of stable isotopes.
moments.takeaway: Stable isotopes are discovered. The atom of an element has variants.

moments.title: Aston's mass spectrograph
moments.body: Aston refines Thomson's instrument and discovers 212 of the 287 naturally occurring isotopes. He wins the 1922 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Most of the periodic table has multiple isotopes.

moments.title: Soft ionisation
moments.body: MALDI and electrospray let mass spec analyse intact proteins and DNA without fragmenting them. Tanaka and Fenn share the 2002 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Mass spectrometry can now weigh biomolecules.

moments.title: Proteomics and metabolomics
moments.body: High-resolution mass spec routinely identifies thousands of proteins from a single sample. COVID-19 vaccines were characterised by mass spec.
moments.takeaway: Mass spec is now the workhorse of pharmaceutical and clinical chemistry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Modern Orbitrap and FT-ICR mass spectrometers reach resolving power > 10^6. Single-cell proteomics is emerging. Forensic mass spec identifies drugs at sub-nanogram levels.
now.open_questions: Can single-molecule mass spec become quantitative? Can MS image proteins in tissue at high resolution?

items.reflection: Aston discovered 212 isotopes by hand. Modern instruments find them in seconds. Has automation changed what 'discovery' means?

moments.title: EPA's green chemistry programme
moments.body: Anastas coins 'green chemistry' at the US EPA. The aim: chemical processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances.
moments.takeaway: Chemistry takes responsibility for its environmental footprint.

moments.title: Twelve Principles
moments.body: Their book 'Green Chemistry: Theory and Practice' sets out 12 principles: atom economy, less hazardous synthesis, renewable feedstocks, etc. The principles become standard teaching.
moments.takeaway: A 12-point manifesto for sustainable chemistry.

moments.title: Olefin metathesis Nobel
moments.body: Catalysts for olefin metathesis enable green synthesis routes with high atom economy. The 2005 Nobel explicitly cites the contribution to green chemistry.
moments.takeaway: Catalysis becomes the engine of green chemistry.

moments.title: Circular chemistry
moments.body: Chemical recycling of plastics, CO2 utilisation, electrochemical synthesis with renewable electricity, and bio-based feedstocks are major research areas. The 12 principles guide design.
moments.takeaway: Chemistry is being reinvented to fit within planetary limits.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Green chemistry is now a standard MSc/PhD topic. Industry routinely uses E-factor (waste/product) as a metric. Green pharma is a multi-billion-dollar industry.
now.open_questions: Can chemistry's emissions reach net-zero by 2050? Can plastics be made fully circular?

items.reflection: Chemistry created the pollution problems and now is being asked to solve them. Can the same discipline that caused the harm cure it?

moments.title: Graphite theory
moments.body: Wallace, while at McGill, derives the band structure of graphite, including its peculiar Dirac-like electronic dispersion. Almost no one notices for 50 years.
moments.takeaway: The exotic electronic structure of graphene is calculated decades before it is isolated.

moments.title: Buckminsterfullerene
moments.body: In a vacuum chamber simulating carbon-rich stellar atmospheres, the team detects C60 — a soccer-ball-shaped carbon molecule. 1996 Nobel. The carbon nanotube (1991) follows.
moments.takeaway: Carbon allotropes proliferate.

moments.title: Sticky-tape graphene
moments.body: On 'Friday evening experiments', Geim and Novoselov peel graphite with Scotch tape, leaving single-layer graphene flakes. They measure their electronic properties. 2010 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: The first 2D material is isolated with adhesive tape.

moments.title: 2D materials zoo
moments.body: Hexagonal boron nitride, transition-metal dichalcogenides, twisted bilayer graphene (showing flat bands and superconductivity) — a whole new class of materials emerges.
moments.takeaway: Sticky-tape graphene launches a decade-long boom in 2D materials.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Graphene is in batteries, composites, sensors, and (occasionally) display technology. Commercial uptake has been slower than the hype but real. Twisted bilayer 'magic-angle' graphene is a hot research area.
now.open_questions: Can graphene replace silicon in any major electronic application?

items.reflection: Geim and Novoselov won a Nobel for an experiment any school student could try. What separates a 'Friday-evening experiment' from a Nobel-winning insight?

moments.title: Whittingham's first Li battery
moments.body: Working at an oil company concerned about peak oil, Whittingham builds a lithium-titanium disulphide battery. The cells short and catch fire. Exxon abandons the project after the oil shock recedes.
moments.takeaway: The lithium-ion concept is born at an oil company, then dropped.

moments.title: Cobalt oxide cathode
moments.body: Goodenough finds that LiCoO2 is a stable, high-voltage cathode. The fundamental chemistry of modern Li-ion is fixed.
moments.takeaway: The cathode material that powers your phone is invented in Oxford.

moments.title: Graphite anode
moments.body: Yoshino combines LiCoO2 with a carbon (graphite) anode, eliminating metallic lithium and making cells safe enough to commercialise. Sony launches the first commercial Li-ion battery in 1991.
moments.takeaway: Combining the right cathode and anode produces a billion-unit-per-year technology.

moments.title: Nobel for Li-ion
moments.body: The three share the 2019 chemistry Nobel. Goodenough at 97 is the oldest ever Nobel laureate.
moments.takeaway: Li-ion finally wins the recognition it deserves.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Li-ion batteries power phones, laptops, and an exploding electric-vehicle market. Production is ~3 TWh/year (2025). Solid-state batteries are emerging.
now.open_questions: Can solid-state Li batteries become commercial? What replaces cobalt and nickel?

items.reflection: Goodenough won a Nobel at 97, after decades of being overlooked. Why does recognition come so late to some, so easily to others?

moments.title: Strange repeats in E. coli
moments.body: Japanese researchers find unusual repeated sequences in E. coli DNA. They have no idea what the function is. Similar repeats are found in many bacteria over the next 15 years.
moments.takeaway: A mysterious genomic pattern, ignored for decades.

moments.title: CRISPR as bacterial immunity
moments.body: Yogurt-company researchers show CRISPR is a bacterial defence system — the bacteria record viral DNA fragments to recognise reinfection. Adaptive immunity in bacteria.
moments.takeaway: Industrial yoghurt research uncovers bacterial immunity.

moments.title: Doudna and Charpentier reprogramme CRISPR
moments.body: Doudna (Berkeley) and Charpentier (Sweden) show CRISPR-Cas9 can be programmed with a single guide RNA to cut any DNA sequence. They share the 2020 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Bacterial immunity is repurposed into a universal genome-editing tool.

moments.title: First CRISPR therapy approved
moments.body: Casgevy, a CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease, is approved in the UK and US. The first CRISPR-edited human treatments enter the clinic.
moments.takeaway: A bacterial immune system, repurposed, cures human disease.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: CRISPR is used in research, agriculture and medicine. Base editing and prime editing extend the toolkit. Off-target effects and germ-line editing raise major ethical issues.
now.open_questions: Should germline gene editing be permitted? Can CRISPR cure HIV, cancer, inherited disease?

items.reflection: He Jiankui used CRISPR on human embryos in 2018 and was jailed. Doudna and Charpentier urged a moratorium. When should science self-regulate vs accept external rules?

moments.title: Werner's coordination theory
moments.body: Werner explains why CoCl3·6NH3 behaves differently from Cr(NH3)6Cl3: octahedral coordination spheres around the metal centre. He wins the 1913 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Transition-metal complexes have defined geometries — usually octahedral.

moments.title: Crystal field theory
moments.who: Hans Bethe, then John Van Vleck
moments.body: Bethe and Van Vleck explain transition-metal colours and magnetism via crystal-field splitting of d-orbitals. The colour of copper sulphate gets a quantum-mechanical explanation.
moments.takeaway: Why is copper sulphate blue? Quantum mechanics answers.

moments.title: Ferrocene
moments.body: Ferrocene — an iron atom sandwiched between two cyclopentadienyl rings — is synthesised. Its structure defies classical bonding rules. Wilkinson and Fischer share the 1973 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Organometallic chemistry is born. The boundary between organic and inorganic blurs.

moments.title: Wilkinson's catalyst
moments.body: Wilkinson's RhCl(PPh3)3 catalyses hydrogenation under mild conditions. Homogeneous catalysis becomes a major industrial method.
moments.takeaway: Transition-metal catalysts revolutionise organic chemistry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Transition-metal catalysis (Suzuki, Heck, Negishi 2010 Nobel; metathesis 2005 Nobel) underpins modern drug synthesis. Cisplatin saves thousands of cancer patients annually.
now.open_questions: Can earth-abundant metals (Fe, Co, Ni) replace precious ones (Pt, Pd, Rh, Ir) in catalysis?

items.reflection: Werner married a Catholic and refused to be baptised Lutheran for an academic post — a 19th-century stand for principle. How does professional pressure shape scientific identity?

moments.title: Drake's well
moments.body: Drake drills the first commercial oil well, producing kerosene for lamps (replacing whale oil). The oil age begins.
moments.takeaway: The petroleum industry starts as a substitute for whales.

moments.title: Thermal cracking
moments.body: Burton develops thermal cracking — heating heavy oil under pressure to break it into petrol. Petrol output doubles per barrel of crude.
moments.takeaway: Cars become economically viable.

moments.title: Catalytic cracking
moments.body: Houdry's catalytic cracking dramatically improves petrol yield and octane. The high-octane fuel enables WWII aviation; without it, the Allies could not have produced enough fighter and bomber fuel.
moments.takeaway: A French chemist's catalyst arguably wins the air war.

moments.title: Energy transition
moments.body: Crude oil refining is being squeezed by EVs and renewable feedstocks. Major refineries are converting to bio-fuels, plastics, and synthetic chemicals.
moments.takeaway: The petrochemical industry is being slowly redirected.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Global oil consumption: ~100 million barrels/day. Plastics from oil: ~400 Mt/year. Refining accounts for ~5% of global energy use.
now.open_questions: Can the petrochemical industry transition to net-zero by 2050? Will biomass feedstocks scale?

items.reflection: Refining gave us cheap fuel — and CO2-driven climate change. Does the same chemistry that enables modernity threaten it?

moments.title: Rosenberg's accidental cure
moments.body: Rosenberg studies how electric currents affect bacterial growth. The cells stop dividing — not because of electricity, but because of platinum compounds leaching from his electrodes. The same compounds turn out to kill cancer cells.
moments.takeaway: A bacterial-growth experiment serendipitously discovers a leading cancer drug.

moments.title: Cisplatin approved
moments.body: Cisplatin is approved for testicular and ovarian cancer. Testicular cancer survival jumps from <10% to >90%. Lance Armstrong is one of millions whose lives are saved.
moments.takeaway: A platinum-based drug transforms cancer outcomes.

moments.title: Carboplatin, oxaliplatin
moments.body: Carboplatin (1989) and oxaliplatin (2002) reduce cisplatin's toxic side effects. Platinum drugs become a >$2 billion/year market.
moments.takeaway: Whole drug classes follow from one serendipitous discovery.

moments.title: Mechanism still studied
moments.body: Cisplatin's mechanism — DNA cross-linking — is well established, but exactly why some tumours respond and others don't is still being unravelled.
moments.takeaway: Mechanism understanding lags clinical use by decades.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Cisplatin is one of the WHO essential medicines. Platinum compounds are in roughly half of all cancer chemotherapy regimens worldwide.
now.open_questions: Why do some cancers resist cisplatin? Can next-generation Pt drugs target tumours selectively?

items.reflection: Rosenberg was studying bacteria, not cancer. How much medicine comes from accidental discoveries?

moments.title: Lavoisier overthrows phlogiston
moments.body: Lavoisier shows combustion is reaction with oxygen, not loss of phlogiston. He proves conservation of mass with precise balances. In 1789 he publishes 'Traité élémentaire de chimie', the first modern chemistry textbook.
moments.takeaway: Modern chemistry begins with the balance and the elements list.

moments.title: The guillotine
moments.body: During the Reign of Terror, Lavoisier — a former tax collector — is guillotined. The judge reportedly says: 'The Republic has no need of scholars.' Lagrange remarks: 'It took them only a moment to cut off his head, but a hundred years won't suffice to produce one like it.'
moments.takeaway: The father of modern chemistry is executed by his own country.

moments.title: Lavoisier's wife and posthumous credit
moments.body: Lavoisier's wife, who translated English chemistry, illustrated his treatise, and ran his lab, publishes his memoirs in 1805. She ensures his work is remembered.
moments.takeaway: Marie-Anne Paulze preserves the chemical revolution.

moments.title: Lavoisier's elements
moments.body: Lavoisier listed 33 elements; we know 118. Conservation of mass is still the foundation of stoichiometry — though Einstein in 1905 will show it is part of mass-energy conservation.
moments.takeaway: Lavoisier's framework still holds, with corrections.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Modern chemistry retains Lavoisier's conservation laws and methodology. The IUPAC periodic table descends from his elements list.
now.open_questions: Will any heavier transactinide elements ever be stable enough to study chemically?

items.reflection: Lavoisier was killed by a revolution he supported. How should scientists relate to political upheaval?

moments.title: Boyle's law
moments.body: Boyle (and his assistant Robert Hooke) build an air pump and a J-tube. They show that PV is constant at constant T. Boyle's 'Sceptical Chymist' (1661) attacks Aristotelian elements.
moments.takeaway: The first quantitative gas law — and a manifesto for experimental chemistry.

moments.title: Charles's law
moments.body: Charles shows V/T is constant at constant pressure. Gay-Lussac in 1802 quantifies it. The combined gas law follows.
moments.takeaway: Volume scales with absolute temperature.

moments.title: Clapeyron's combined law
moments.body: Clapeyron combines Boyle, Charles and Avogadro into PV = nRT — the ideal gas law.
moments.takeaway: One equation captures the macroscopic behaviour of dilute gases.

moments.title: Van der Waals correction
moments.body: Van der Waals adds terms for molecular volume and intermolecular forces, giving an equation that works near liquefaction. He wins the 1910 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Real gases need corrections — the first for non-ideality.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The ideal gas law underpins SCUBA diving, weather, internal combustion engines, gas chromatography and modern thermodynamics teaching.
now.open_questions: How accurately can equations of state predict supercritical fluid behaviour?

items.reflection: Boyle's air pump cost a fortune; today every schoolchild does PV calculations. How does technology democratise scientific concepts?

moments.title: Liebig's combustion analysis
moments.body: Liebig perfects combustion analysis — burning an organic compound to determine its C, H, O content. He sets up the first modern teaching laboratory at Giessen and trains a generation of chemists.
moments.takeaway: Quantitative organic chemistry — and the first chemistry teaching lab — emerge.

moments.title: Liebig's mineral fertiliser
moments.body: Liebig proves plants need nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK), not 'humus'. He launches the artificial fertiliser industry.
moments.takeaway: Modern agriculture begins with a chemist's analysis of plant ash.

moments.title: Liebig's Extract of Meat
moments.body: Liebig commercialises a beef-extract product, predecessor to OXO and stock cubes. He also gives his name to the Liebig condenser, still standard in every chemistry lab.
moments.takeaway: A chemist becomes a household name through fertilisers and stock cubes.

moments.title: NPK feeds the world
moments.body: Roughly 200 Mt of N fertiliser per year (mainly Haber-Bosch) feeds half of humanity. NPK runoff also drives ocean dead zones.
moments.takeaway: Liebig's fertilisers feed the planet — and pollute it.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Precision agriculture, slow-release fertilisers and microbial-based N fixation are major research areas to reduce fertiliser overuse.
now.open_questions: Can we replace synthetic fertilisers with biological N-fixation?

items.reflection: Liebig's fertilisers saved billions from hunger and damaged the global nitrogen cycle. Are some inventions both irreversibly good and bad?

moments.title: Moseley's law
moments.body: Moseley, 26, shows X-ray frequencies from elements scale with nuclear charge — atomic number, not atomic weight. He reorders Co-Ni and Te-I in the periodic table and shows there are exactly 4 gaps (elements 43, 61, 72, 75) still to find.
moments.takeaway: Atomic number, not atomic weight, organises the periodic table.

moments.title: Moseley dies at Gallipoli
moments.body: Moseley enlists despite Rutherford's pleas; he is killed by a sniper at Gallipoli at age 27. Asimov later writes: 'In view of what he might still have accomplished, his death might well have been the most costly single death of the War to mankind generally.'
moments.takeaway: One of the most promising scientists of his generation, killed at 27.

moments.title: Britain's Pittsburgh policy
moments.body: After Moseley's death, the UK introduces a policy of never assigning prominent scientists to combat roles. The policy holds in WWII.
moments.takeaway: A single death changes military policy.

moments.title: The four missing elements
moments.body: Technetium (43, 1937), promethium (61, 1945), hafnium (72, 1923), rhenium (75, 1925) are all eventually found — exactly the gaps Moseley predicted.
moments.takeaway: Moseley's table is verified, element by element.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The periodic table is now ordered by atomic number. Synchrotron X-ray sources continue Moseley's tradition. He is generally considered to have lost a clear Nobel due to his death.
now.open_questions: Will element 119 (ununennium) ever be confirmed? How is the periodic table best extended?

items.reflection: Moseley's death at 27 cost the world incalculable science. How should states protect scientists during war?

moments.title: Buchner's cell-free fermentation
moments.body: Buchner crushes yeast cells and shows the extract still ferments sugar. The 'vital force' isn't necessary — fermentation is enzymatic chemistry. 1907 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Biochemistry leaves vitalism behind.

moments.title: Sumner crystallises urease
moments.body: Sumner, who had lost his left arm in a hunting accident, crystallises the enzyme urease from jack beans. He shows enzymes are proteins. The chemistry establishment (especially Willstätter) refuses to believe him. He wins the 1946 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: A one-armed chemist proves enzymes are proteins — and is disbelieved for two decades.

moments.title: Myoglobin structure
moments.body: Kendrew solves the structure of myoglobin by X-ray crystallography — the first protein structure. Perutz solves haemoglobin years later. 1962 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Proteins have 3D structures that can be solved at atomic resolution.

moments.title: AlphaFold
moments.body: AlphaFold predicts protein structures from sequence with near-experimental accuracy. The team releases predictions for ~200 million proteins. Hassabis and Jumper share the 2024 Chemistry Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Computational biology now rivals X-ray crystallography in solving protein structures.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: AlphaFold has provided structures for almost every protein in known biology. Cryo-EM (2017 Nobel) provides experimental complement. Enzyme engineering is now structure-guided.
now.open_questions: Can we now design enzymes for arbitrary reactions from sequence?

items.reflection: Sumner was disbelieved for 20 years; Hassabis solved the same problem with AI. How does technology change what we trust?

moments.title: Grignard's PhD
moments.body: Grignard, a doctoral student of Philippe Barbier, finds that magnesium reacts with alkyl halides in dry ether to form 'RMgX' — what we now call Grignard reagents. They react with carbonyls to form new carbon-carbon bonds.
moments.takeaway: A simple reagent that builds C-C bonds reliably.

moments.title: Grignard wins Nobel
moments.body: Grignard wins the 1912 Nobel with Sabatier (catalytic hydrogenation). His advisor Barbier is omitted, despite providing the original insight.
moments.takeaway: Grignard wins; his advisor is forgotten.

moments.title: Industrial-scale C-C bonds
moments.body: Grignard reactions remain a primary tool for C-C bond formation in pharmaceutical synthesis. They appear in production of statins, antihistamines, vitamins.
moments.takeaway: Over a century later, Grignard reagents are still in active industrial use.

moments.title: Cross-coupling
moments.body: Pd-catalysed cross-coupling reactions (Negishi, Suzuki-Miyaura, Heck) extend organometallic C-C bond formation; 2010 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Organometallic chemistry now dominates pharmaceutical synthesis.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Cross-coupling and organometallic C-C bond formation are arguably the most important reactions in modern pharmaceutical synthesis.
now.open_questions: Can earth-abundant metals (Fe, Cu, Ni) match Pd in cross-coupling efficiency?

items.reflection: Grignard's advisor Barbier was omitted from the Nobel. Why do advisors so often vanish from the citation history?

moments.title: Hess's law
moments.body: A Swiss-Russian chemist publishes the law of constant heat summation: the enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of pathway. The result is years before the first law of thermodynamics is formulated.
moments.takeaway: A practical consequence of energy conservation, derived empirically before the principle.

moments.title: Gibbs free energy
moments.body: Gibbs publishes the chemical potential and Gibbs free energy G = H - TS. The most powerful concept in physical chemistry. Maxwell sends a plaster cast of Gibbs's thermodynamic surface to Yale.
moments.takeaway: The thermodynamic conditions for spontaneous reaction get a single equation.

moments.title: Nernst equation
moments.body: Nernst derives E = E° - (RT/nF) ln Q for the cell potential. Electrochemistry meets thermodynamics. 1920 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Battery voltages can now be calculated from thermodynamics.

moments.title: Third law
moments.body: Nernst's heat theorem (3rd law of thermodynamics): entropy approaches a constant (zero for a perfect crystal) as T → 0 K. Absolute entropy is finally computable.
moments.takeaway: Thermodynamics is closed by a third law.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Modern thermochemistry tables let chemists predict reaction enthalpies and Gibbs free energies for billions of reactions. Computational thermochemistry achieves chemical accuracy (1 kcal/mol).
now.open_questions: Can thermochemical data be predicted reliably from first principles for arbitrary molecules?

items.reflection: Hess derived his law before the first law of thermodynamics. How often does practical chemistry pre-empt deeper theory?

moments.title: Markovnikov's rule
moments.body: Markovnikov publishes a rule for HX addition to alkenes: H adds to the C with more Hs already. The rule is dismissed by Western chemists for years because it appears in Russian journals.
moments.takeaway: A regioselectivity rule, hidden in Russian literature for a generation.

moments.title: Mechanism explained
moments.body: Whitmore explains Markovnikov in terms of carbocation stability. The more stable carbocation forms, controlling the addition.
moments.takeaway: A rule of observation gets a mechanistic basis.

moments.title: Hydroboration
moments.body: Brown develops hydroboration-oxidation, giving anti-Markovnikov hydration of alkenes. He wins the 1979 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: The reverse selectivity becomes achievable.

moments.title: Selective synthesis
moments.body: Modern catalysts let synthetic chemists choose Markovnikov or anti-Markovnikov at will. The 'rule' is now a starting point, not a constraint.
moments.takeaway: Selectivity is now a tunable parameter.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Markovnikov is taught at A-level and IB. The underlying carbocation logic predicts countless other reactions.
now.open_questions: Can we control regiochemistry, stereochemistry and chemoselectivity in arbitrary reactions?

items.reflection: Markovnikov's rule was dismissed for years because it was in Russian. How does language barrier still distort science today?

moments.title: Sørensen at the Carlsberg Lab
moments.body: Working at the Carlsberg Laboratory — set up by the brewery to investigate beer chemistry — Sørensen defines pH = -log[H+] to monitor fermentation acidity. He also coins the terms 'buffer' and 'titration curve'.
moments.takeaway: Beer brewing gives us the most-used scale in chemistry.

moments.title: Glass electrode
moments.body: The glass pH electrode is developed, allowing routine potentiometric pH measurement. By 1934 it is commercial.
moments.takeaway: pH can now be measured at the push of a button.

moments.title: Henderson-Hasselbalch
moments.body: The buffer equation pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) is formalised. Buffer design becomes systematic.
moments.takeaway: Blood pH (7.4 ± 0.05) and protein function get a thermodynamic explanation.

moments.title: Ocean acidification
moments.body: Ocean surface pH has dropped from ~8.2 to ~8.1 since 1750 — a 30% increase in H+ concentration. Coral reefs and pteropods are threatened.
moments.takeaway: pH chemistry tracks one of climate change's most measurable consequences.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: pH is measured in soil, blood, ocean and beer. Continuous monitoring is now standard. pH-sensitive drugs (gastroprotective, GI imaging) exploit the scale.
now.open_questions: How will ocean acidification cascade through marine food webs?

items.reflection: A pH scale invented for beer now measures climate change. How often do industrial measurements become planetary ones?

moments.title: Donora deaths
moments.body: A temperature inversion traps industrial smoke in Donora; 20 die, thousands are hospitalised. The disaster prompts the first US air-quality regulation.
moments.takeaway: Air pollution kills. Quickly.

moments.title: Great Smog of London
moments.body: A four-day coal smog kills an estimated 12,000 Londoners. Parliament passes the Clean Air Act 1956. Coal smoke becomes regulated.
moments.takeaway: The deadliest air-pollution event in modern history.

moments.title: Haagen-Smit identifies photochemical smog
moments.body: Working on LA's brownish smog, Dutch chemist Haagen-Smit shows it forms from NOx and hydrocarbons reacting under sunlight to form ozone. Auto exhaust, not industry, is the main source.
moments.takeaway: Modern smog chemistry is born. The car is the culprit.

moments.title: Catalytic converters
moments.body: Three-way catalytic converters (Pt-Rh-Pd) remove NOx, CO and unburnt hydrocarbons. Combined with low-sulphur fuel, they cut urban smog dramatically — but climate-warming CO2 from fossil cars remains.
moments.takeaway: Atmospheric chemistry guides emission regulation.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Air pollution kills ~7 million people per year (WHO). PM2.5 from cooking, traffic and industry is the leading environmental cause of death. Many low-income cities still exceed safe limits.
now.open_questions: Can global air-quality reach WHO limits while economies grow?

items.reflection: Haagen-Smit's smog identification took years to be believed. Why is detective work in atmospheric chemistry so slow to translate into policy?

moments.title: Pasteur's tartrate crystals
moments.body: Pasteur, 26, separates two types of tartrate crystal by hand under a microscope. They rotate polarised light in opposite directions. He has discovered molecular chirality.
moments.takeaway: Molecules can come in mirror-image forms. Chemistry has handedness.

moments.title: Tetrahedral carbon
moments.who: Jacobus van't Hoff (Utrecht), Achille Le Bel (Paris)
moments.body:
At 22, van't Hoff publishes a 12-page pamphlet proposing carbon is tetrahedral, explaining Pasteur's optical activity. Le Bel proposes the same independently. The chemist Kolbe attacks the idea as 'a fancy notion devoid of any substantial basis'.

van't Hoff wins the first chemistry Nobel in 1901.
moments.takeaway: 3D chemistry is born. The doubters lose.

moments.title: Conformational analysis
moments.body: Barton and Hassel show that ring conformations (chair, boat) control reactivity. They share the 1969 Nobel. Conformational analysis becomes essential for understanding sugars, steroids, drugs.
moments.takeaway: 3D dynamics matter as much as 3D structure.

moments.title: Thalidomide tragedy
moments.body: Thalidomide, sold as a racemic mixture, causes ~10,000 birth defects worldwide. One enantiomer is a sedative; the other is teratogenic. The disaster reshapes drug regulation.
moments.takeaway: Chirality matters. Modern drug development tests each enantiomer.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Asymmetric synthesis (Sharpless, Noyori, Knowles 2001 Nobel; List, MacMillan 2021 Nobel) lets chemists make single enantiomers at scale. Most modern drugs are single enantiomers.
now.open_questions: Why is biological chirality universal — all life uses L-amino acids and D-sugars?

items.reflection: Kolbe ridiculed van't Hoff's tetrahedral carbon. How can communities tell promising new ideas from dead ends?

moments.title: Ingold and Hughes formalise
moments.body: At UCL, Ingold and Hughes formalise the SN1/SN2 (and E1/E2) classification of organic reaction mechanisms. They derive rate laws and stereochemical signatures for each. Curly arrows enter undergraduate teaching.
moments.takeaway: Organic mechanisms become systematic.

moments.title: Walden inversion explained
moments.body: Hughes and Ingold show SN2 produces inversion of configuration at the stereo centre — explaining the Walden inversion known since 1896. They distinguish 'frontside' vs 'backside' attack.
moments.takeaway: Stereochemical outcomes follow from mechanism.

moments.title: Hughes-Ingold rules
moments.body: Their book systematises solvent and substrate effects on SN1/SN2. The Hughes-Ingold rules predict which mechanism dominates.
moments.takeaway: Mechanism is now predictable from substrate and conditions.

moments.title: Mechanism by computation
moments.body: DFT calculations now compute transition-state energies for arbitrary reactions, predicting selectivity and yield before lab work begins.
moments.takeaway: Curly arrows have become quantum chemistry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: SN1, SN2, E1, E2 are universal teaching frameworks. Modern computation extends to enzymes, materials, polymers.
now.open_questions: Can we computationally predict reaction yields and selectivities for arbitrary substrates?

items.reflection: Curly arrows are a 1930s graphical convention. They remain the universal language of organic chemistry. Why have they not been replaced by something more rigorous?

moments.title: Latimer and Rodebush
moments.body: Two Berkeley graduate students propose the 'hydrogen bond' to explain anomalous properties of water and HF. The paper is rejected by their advisor G. N. Lewis, who later publishes the idea.
moments.takeaway: The hydrogen bond is named, then nearly suppressed by an advisor.

moments.title: Pauling formalises
moments.body: In 'The Nature of the Chemical Bond', Pauling gives the hydrogen bond its modern framework. He proposes it underlies water's unique behaviour, protein structure, and DNA pairing (later).
moments.takeaway: H-bonding becomes a central concept across chemistry and biology.

moments.title: DNA base pairing
moments.body: Watson-Crick base pairing — A-T, G-C — relies on hydrogen bonds. Without H-bonds, DNA cannot replicate. Heredity rests on this weakest of bonds.
moments.takeaway: Life depends on hydrogen bonds.

moments.title: H-bonding in catalysis
moments.body: Hydrogen-bond donors (thioureas, squaramides) catalyse asymmetric reactions. Bonds 'too weak to matter' make industrial-scale enantioselectivity.
moments.takeaway: Hydrogen bonds are the workhorse of modern asymmetric catalysis.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Hydrogen bonding explains water's anomalies, protein folding, DNA replication, sapphire's hardness, and asymmetric catalysis. It is omnipresent in chemistry teaching.
now.open_questions: What is the limit of hydrogen-bond strength? Can engineered H-bond networks rival covalent bonds in toughness?

items.reflection: Lewis suppressed his students' hydrogen-bond paper before publishing the idea. How often does priority disputes obscure credit?

moments.title: Wittig's reaction
moments.body: Wittig discovers that phosphorus ylides convert ketones and aldehydes to alkenes in one step — predictable, reliable, stereospecific. He wins the 1979 Nobel with H. C. Brown.
moments.takeaway: A versatile new route to alkenes.

moments.title: Vitamin A industrial synthesis
moments.body: BASF launches industrial vitamin A synthesis using a Wittig step. Hundreds of tonnes per year of vitamin A are now made this way.
moments.takeaway: The Wittig becomes industrial chemistry.

moments.title: Variants
moments.body: Variants (HWE — Horner-Wadsworth-Emmons; Schlosser modification) give selective E or Z alkenes. The Wittig family covers most synthetic needs.
moments.takeaway: Wittig and its variants give complete control of alkene geometry.

moments.title: In drug discovery
moments.body: The Wittig appears in countless total syntheses and pharmaceutical preparations. Discodermolide, taxol — landmark natural products — use it.
moments.takeaway: Wittig is a foundational reaction in modern synthesis.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Wittig and its cousins remain among the most-used reactions in organic synthesis. Pd-catalysed cross-couplings now compete for some applications.
now.open_questions: Can a fully catalytic, atom-economical Wittig be developed?

items.reflection: Wittig discovered a reaction in 1953; it became industrial within 5 years. Why are some discoveries adopted so quickly?

moments.title: Nicholson and Carlisle electrolyse water
moments.body: Days after Volta's pile is described in print, Nicholson and Carlisle use one to electrolyse water into H2 and O2. The first electrochemical decomposition.
moments.takeaway: Within weeks of the first battery, water is split into its elements.

moments.title: Faraday's laws
moments.body: Faraday formulates his two laws of electrolysis: mass deposited is proportional to charge, and to equivalent weight. Electrochemistry becomes quantitative.
moments.takeaway: Electrochemistry gets its fundamental laws.

moments.title: Hall-Héroult aluminium
moments.body: Simultaneously and independently, two 22-year-olds develop the electrolytic process for aluminium. Aluminium goes from precious metal (Napoleon's banquet plates) to cheap commodity within a decade.
moments.takeaway: Aluminium becomes a mass commodity through electrolysis.

moments.title: Green hydrogen
moments.body: Electrolysers powered by renewable electricity produce green H2 for steel, ammonia, transport. Scale-up to GW-class plants is happening in 2024-2030.
moments.takeaway: Electrolysis may yet decarbonise heavy industry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Electrolysis is being scaled massively for green H2. PEM and alkaline electrolysers compete; solid-oxide and AEM emerging. Catalysis improvements reduce iridium and platinum use.
now.open_questions: Can green H2 be produced at cost-competitive levels by 2030?

items.reflection: Hall and Héroult independently solved aluminium electrolysis in the same year. How often does technology emerge when its time comes?

moments.title: Photo 51
moments.who: Rosalind Franklin, Raymond Gosling, King's College London
moments.body: Franklin and her PhD student Gosling take 'Photo 51' — an X-ray diffraction image of B-form DNA. The pattern reveals helical structure with 3.4 Å spacing.
moments.takeaway: The clearest evidence of DNA's helix yet captured.

moments.title: Photo 51 shown without permission
moments.body: Wilkins shows Photo 51 to Watson without Franklin's consent. Watson and Crick complete their model within weeks. Their Nature paper credits Franklin in a brief footnote.
moments.takeaway: A landmark structure derived from a colleague's data, shared without consent.

moments.title: Franklin dies at 37
moments.body: Franklin dies of ovarian cancer at 37 — possibly induced by her X-ray exposure. The Nobel rules prohibit posthumous awards; the 1962 Nobel goes to Watson, Crick and Wilkins.
moments.takeaway: Franklin dies before she can be recognised. Whether she would have shared the Nobel had she lived is hotly debated.

moments.title: Reassessment
moments.body: Franklin's role has been progressively re-evaluated. Modern scholarship establishes her as a co-discoverer, not just a data provider. Statues, prizes, buildings now bear her name.
moments.takeaway: Historical credit is being rebalanced — too late for Franklin to know.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: DNA double helix is the icon of modern biology. Modern DNA structure determination uses sequencing rather than crystallography. Franklin's other work on viruses and coal also stands as major contribution.
now.open_questions: How should institutions correct historical injustices in scientific credit?

items.reflection: Watson called Franklin 'Rosy' (which she hated) in his memoir and described her in patronising terms. He later wrote a partial apology. When does a memoir become history?

moments.title: Grotthuss law
moments.body: Grotthuss formulates the law that only absorbed light produces chemical change. Stark in 1900 quantifies it: one photon per molecule.
moments.takeaway: The first law of photochemistry.

moments.title: Becquerel's photoelectric cell
moments.body: At 19, Becquerel observes that light produces a voltage at certain electrodes — the photovoltaic effect. He misses the Nobel but his son Henri later wins one for radioactivity.
moments.takeaway: Sunlight to electricity — a 184-year project begins.

moments.title: Calvin's photosynthesis tracer studies
moments.body: Calvin uses radioactive 14C and 2D paper chromatography to trace photosynthesis. He maps the Calvin cycle. 1961 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Photosynthesis is decoded by isotope tracing.

moments.title: Femtochemistry
moments.body: Zewail uses femtosecond laser pulses to image molecules as they react. He watches bonds break and form. 1999 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Chemistry can now be watched in real time at the femtosecond scale.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Photocatalysis, attosecond spectroscopy, photovoltaic cells (now 20-30% efficient), photodynamic therapy and photoredox catalysis all derive from photochemistry foundations. Solar cells generate ~10% of global electricity.
now.open_questions: Can artificial photosynthesis approach natural efficiency? Can attosecond science image electron dynamics in solids?

items.reflection: Becquerel discovered the photovoltaic effect in 1839 — it took 150 years to become a major energy source. Why such long delays from discovery to deployment?

moments.title: Berzelius names catalysis
moments.body: Berzelius coins the term 'catalysis' for reactions where a substance influences without being consumed. The concept was previously fuzzy.
moments.takeaway: Catalysis becomes a recognised category of chemistry.

moments.title: Sabatier's hydrogenation
moments.body: Sabatier finds finely divided nickel hydrogenates olefins. The technique becomes industrial: margarine, cooking oils, petrochemicals. 1912 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Heterogeneous catalysis becomes a major industry.

moments.title: Haber-Bosch
moments.body: Iron catalyst at high temperature and pressure makes ammonia from N2 and H2. Haber 1918 Nobel; Bosch 1931 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: The most important industrial reaction ever — feeding the world.

moments.title: Fischer-Tropsch and beyond
moments.who: Franz Fischer, Hans Tropsch; Mittasch; etc.
moments.body: Fischer-Tropsch (1925) turns syngas into liquid fuels. Catalysts now mediate ~90% of industrial chemical products.
moments.takeaway: Modern industry rests on heterogeneous catalysis.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Catalysis accounts for ~35% of global GDP. Modern catalysts use rare metals; the field is racing to replace them. Single-atom catalysis is a major frontier.
now.open_questions: Can earth-abundant catalysts replace platinum-group metals in catalytic converters and electrolysers?

items.reflection: Catalysis is invisible but essential. Sabatier, Haber, Bosch — all chemists who shaped the modern world. Why is industrial chemistry so under-celebrated?

moments.title: Heck reaction
moments.body: Heck shows palladium can couple aryl halides with alkenes. The first general Pd-catalysed C-C coupling.
moments.takeaway: Palladium catalysis becomes synthetic chemistry's new workhorse.

moments.title: Negishi coupling
moments.body: Negishi develops a Pd-catalysed coupling using organozincs. He shares the 2010 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Pd cross-coupling becomes general.

moments.title: Suzuki-Miyaura coupling
moments.body: Suzuki and Miyaura develop a Pd-catalysed coupling of organoboronic acids with aryl halides. The reaction is air- and water-tolerant, easy, scalable. It becomes the most-used metal-catalysed reaction in pharma.
moments.takeaway: The Suzuki coupling is arguably the most consequential reaction in modern drug synthesis.

moments.title: Nobel for cross-coupling
moments.body: The 2010 Nobel goes to the three cross-coupling pioneers. Buchwald and Hartwig develop further variants (C-N coupling). Pd cross-coupling now appears in ~25% of pharma syntheses.
moments.takeaway: Pd cross-coupling has reshaped how chemistry is done in industry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Pd cross-coupling is everywhere in pharma. Ni and Cu alternatives are advancing. C-H activation is the next frontier.
now.open_questions: Can we replace Pd with earth-abundant Ni or Fe in cross-coupling at industrial scale?

items.reflection: Three independent groups developed Pd cross-coupling within years of each other. When does a discovery become inevitable?

moments.title: Cosmic ray N-14
moments.body: Korff discovers cosmic-ray neutrons produce 14C from atmospheric 14N. The radioactive isotope (half-life 5,730 years) mixes through the biosphere.
moments.takeaway: A natural radioisotope is continuously made in the atmosphere.

moments.title: Libby develops radiocarbon dating
moments.body: Libby measures 14C in biological samples and calibrates against tree rings. Living things have a known 14C content; dead samples lose it predictably. 1960 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Archaeology becomes quantitative.

moments.title: Dead Sea Scrolls dated
moments.body: Radiocarbon dating confirms the Dead Sea Scrolls are 2,000 years old. Public attention on the technique surges.
moments.takeaway: Radiocarbon dating becomes culturally famous.

moments.title: AMS dating
moments.body: AMS measures 14C atom by atom, needing milligrams instead of grams. Iceman 'Ötzi' is dated (~5,300 years). Even microscopic samples can now be dated.
moments.takeaway: Radiocarbon dating becomes microscale.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Radiocarbon underpins prehistoric archaeology, climate science, art authentication, forensic medicine. The 'bomb spike' from 1950s nuclear tests is a globally calibrated marker.
now.open_questions: Can carbon-cycle changes due to fossil fuels still allow accurate dating beyond 2050?

items.reflection: Radiocarbon dating disproved many cultural origin stories; revealed Shroud of Turin as medieval. How do communities respond when chemistry contradicts their narratives?

moments.title: Stone's willow bark
moments.body: Reverend Edward Stone reports that powdered willow bark reduces fever — five grains every four hours. He has rediscovered an ancient remedy (Hippocrates used it).
moments.takeaway: An English clergyman publishes the first scientific report of aspirin's precursor.

moments.title: Salicin to salicylic acid
moments.body: Buchner isolates salicin from willow (1828). Piria converts it to salicylic acid (1839). Kolbe synthesises salicylic acid from phenol (1859) — the first cheap industrial synthesis.
moments.takeaway: A folk remedy becomes industrial chemistry.

moments.title: Bayer's aspirin
moments.body:
Bayer chemists acetylate salicylic acid to reduce stomach irritation. Aspirin (Acetyl + Spiraea — the willow genus) is patented in 1899 and becomes the world's first blockbuster drug.

Eichengrün, who later claimed primary credit, was excluded under Nazi-era company history because he was Jewish.
moments.takeaway: The most-used drug in history. Credit erased by Nazi-era historiography.

moments.title: Vane explains the mechanism
moments.body: Vane shows aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX), blocking prostaglandin synthesis. 1982 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Aspirin's mechanism is finally understood — 74 years after introduction.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Aspirin is on the WHO essential medicines list. ~50,000 tonnes are produced annually. It is used as an analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet drug.
now.open_questions: Can low-dose aspirin reduce cancer risk in average-risk adults? Trial results are mixed.

items.reflection: Bayer initially excluded Eichengrün from aspirin's discovery story. How should companies revise corporate history when injustice comes to light?

moments.title: Lind's scurvy trial
moments.body: Royal Navy surgeon James Lind runs one of history's first clinical trials. He gives sailors with scurvy six different treatments. Citrus fruit cures them. The Royal Navy is slow to adopt; it takes 42 years for lemon juice to become standard.
moments.takeaway: The first clinical trial in medicine. The Royal Navy takes 42 years to listen.

moments.title: Funk coins 'vitamine'
moments.body: Polish biochemist Casimir Funk isolates a substance from rice husks that prevents beriberi. He calls it 'vitamine' (vital amine). The 'e' is later dropped when most vitamins turn out not to be amines.
moments.takeaway: Essential micronutrients get a name.

moments.title: Vitamin C synthesis
moments.body: Vitamin C is synthesised at industrial scale. Scurvy is essentially eliminated in industrialised countries.
moments.takeaway: Vitamins become mass-produced commodities.

moments.title: Vitamin B12 structure
moments.body: Hodgkin solves the structure of vitamin B12 by X-ray crystallography — a feat that takes 8 years. She also solves penicillin and insulin. 1964 Nobel — the third woman to win in chemistry.
moments.takeaway: X-ray crystallography solves the most complex small molecule yet.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Thirteen vitamins are recognised. Vitamin deficiencies still kill — vitamin A deficiency causes ~600,000 child deaths per year. Golden Rice is engineered to address this.
