now.open_questions: What are the optimum vitamin levels for long-term health? Megadosing remains controversial.

items.reflection: Lind discovered the scurvy cure; the Royal Navy ignored him for 42 years. How can we shorten the lag between discovery and policy?

moments.title: Leblanc process
moments.body: Leblanc invents a process for sodium carbonate from salt — but using H2SO4 and producing HCl and Ca-sulphide waste. The waste streams choke industrial valleys for a century.
moments.takeaway: The first industrial inorganic process — and the first industrial pollution disaster.

moments.title: Solvay process
moments.body: Solvay's ammonia-soda process recycles ammonia and produces only CaCl2 waste. It displaces Leblanc by 1900.
moments.takeaway: A cleaner industrial process replaces a dirty one.

moments.title: Solvay Conferences endowed
moments.body: Solvay uses his fortune to endow the Solvay Conferences. The 1911 conference launches modern physics; the 1927 conference debates quantum mechanics.
moments.takeaway: Chemical industry profits fund the most important meetings in physics history.

moments.title: Soda ash worldwide
moments.body: Global Na2CO3 production is ~60 Mt/year for glass, detergents, paper, chemicals. The Solvay process still dominates, though synthetic and mining (trona) alternatives exist.
moments.takeaway: Solvay's 160-year-old process still runs at global scale.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Solvay Conferences continue. The 'big-Five' inorganic processes (Solvay, Haber-Bosch, contact, chloralkali, Ostwald) define industrial inorganic chemistry. CO2 emissions are now the dominant criticism.
now.open_questions: Can industrial processes scale electrochemistry instead of high-temperature chemistry?

items.reflection: Solvay's fortune funded the conferences that gave us quantum mechanics. How often does industry-pure research feedback create civilisational leaps?

moments.title: Babylonian soap
moments.body: Babylonian clay tablets record soap-making by boiling animal fats with wood ash. The chemistry is essentially modern saponification, 5,000 years before chemistry is understood.
moments.takeaway: Soap is among humanity's oldest chemical products.

moments.title: Chevreul explains saponification
moments.body: Chevreul (who lived to 102) shows soap is the alkali salt of a fatty acid: triglyceride + NaOH → soap + glycerol. The first quantitative analysis of fats.
moments.takeaway: Soap chemistry becomes systematic. Lipid chemistry is founded.

moments.title: Semmelweis and handwashing
moments.body: Semmelweis shows that hand washing with chlorinated lime cuts maternal mortality dramatically. He is rejected, hospitalised, and dies in an asylum.
moments.takeaway: Soap saves lives; the inventor of clinical hand hygiene dies in obscurity.

moments.title: Soap vs COVID
moments.body: Hand soap, by disrupting the lipid envelope of SARS-CoV-2, is one of the cheapest pandemic interventions. Health authorities worldwide promote hand washing.
moments.takeaway: 5,000-year-old chemistry helps end the worst pandemic in a century.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Modern soap and detergent industry is worth ~$200 billion/year. Surfactants are central to cleaning, oil recovery, cosmetics, and drug formulation.
now.open_questions: How can detergent chemistry be made biodegradable while remaining effective?

items.reflection: Soap is the most consequential cheap chemistry ever. Why is it rarely glamorised in chemistry teaching?

moments.title: First ionic liquid
moments.body: Walden synthesises ethylammonium nitrate, melting at 12°C — the first room-temperature ionic liquid. The class is largely ignored for 80 years.
moments.takeaway: A class of designer solvents is invented in 1914 and shelved.

moments.title: Air-stable ionic liquids
moments.body: Air- and water-stable ionic liquids based on imidazolium cations transform the field. They have negligible vapour pressure and tunable polarity. Green chemistry adopts them eagerly.
moments.takeaway: Designer solvents become practical.

moments.title: Supercritical CO2
moments.body: Coffee decaffeination, dry cleaning, polymer processing — supercritical CO2 replaces toxic solvents. The CO2 is recycled within the process.
moments.takeaway: Carbon dioxide becomes a useful, recyclable solvent.

moments.title: Deep eutectic solvents
moments.body: Deep eutectic solvents (e.g. choline chloride / urea) provide cheap, biodegradable alternatives to ionic liquids. They are used in metal extraction, biomass processing.
moments.takeaway: Solvent design becomes a major thread of green chemistry.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Green solvent research is a major area. Process intensification, water-based reactions, and solvent-free synthesis are all being pushed.
now.open_questions: Can the chemical industry reduce solvent use by 90%?

items.reflection: Walden's ionic liquid was forgotten for 80 years. How many other useful inventions are sitting unused in old literature?

moments.title: Schönbein notices a smell
moments.body: Schönbein, electrolysing water, notices a sharp smell — and names it 'ozone' from the Greek for 'to smell'. He shows it is a strong oxidant. The molecular structure remains unclear for decades.
moments.takeaway: A new oxidant is identified by its smell.

moments.title: Soret shows O3
moments.body: Soret demonstrates that ozone is triatomic oxygen (O3). It is allotropic — same element, different molecular form.
moments.takeaway: Ozone is structurally identified.

moments.title: Stratospheric ozone layer
moments.body: Fabry and Buisson show much of the Sun's UV is absorbed by an ozone layer at 15-35 km altitude. The layer protects all surface life from harmful UV-B and UV-C.
moments.takeaway: Life on land is enabled by atmospheric ozone.

moments.title: Ozone hole confirmed
moments.body: Antarctic stratospheric ozone has dropped 40% — confirming Molina-Rowland predictions about CFCs. Montreal Protocol follows in 1987.
moments.takeaway: Industrial chemicals nearly destroyed the planetary UV shield.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Stratospheric ozone is slowly recovering. Tropospheric (ground-level) ozone, however, is rising in many cities and damaging crops and lungs.
now.open_questions: How will climate-driven changes to stratospheric dynamics affect ozone recovery?

items.reflection: Schönbein smelled ozone in 1839 without knowing what it was. How often do we sense phenomena before naming them?
